claims.text: FeCuCrCoNi high-entropy alloy nanoparticles have a size-dependent thermal response during heating.
The thermal response of FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles can be predicted using large-scale molecular dynamics with a specialized multi-principal-element potential.
The relevant as-synthesized FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles range from a few to tens of nanometers in diameter.
A multicomponent EAM or MEAM potential can be used in classical MD to model the nanoparticles.
Systematically heating the nanoparticles from ambient to elevated temperatures in MD can reveal their thermal evolution.
The simulations should use a controlled temperature ramp and multiple particle sizes.
The simulations should represent vacuum or inert-gas conditions.
Atomistic diffusion and surface segregation are structural mediators of the nanoparticles' thermal response.
Increasing thermal energy promotes surface and interface diffusion among multiple principal elements.
Thermally activated diffusion causes morphological evolution and partial elemental segregation in FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles.
The thermally induced morphological and segregation behavior is size-dependent.
Smaller FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles undergo faster morphological evolution and segregation than larger particles under thermal stress.
High configurational entropy may slow diffusion relative to analogous alloys containing fewer elements.
At low temperatures or in larger particles, configurational-entropy effects slow diffusion and preserve structural stability.
Atomic rearrangements become more pronounced at higher temperatures.
Short MD timescales constrain assessment of size-dependent thermal effects.
Surface passivation may shift the onset or extent of thermal changes.
Exact transition temperatures, timescales, and compositional profiles may be inaccurate when experimental data or long-timescale diffusion behavior are unavailable.
In situ high-temperature TEM or STEM with elemental mapping can test thermally induced morphology and segregation in these nanoparticles.
